stem: Which of the following could NOT be the sum of the measures, in degrees, of four of these eight angles?
stimulus: In a nutrition science study, a cafeteria tray has two parallel straight edges that are crossed by one straight divider. The divider is not perpendicular to the edges, and the two crossings form eight angles. One of the eight angles measures $x^\circ$.
explanation: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, it makes only two different angle measures: $x^\circ$ and $(180 - x)^\circ$. Four of each kind appear. If you pick $b$ angles that measure $180 - x$ and $4 - b$ angles that measure $x$, the sum is $(4 - b)x + b(180 - x)$. For $b = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$, this gives $4x$, $180 + 2x$, $360$, $540 - 2x$, and $720 - 4x$. The expression $360 - 2x$ is not on that list, so it can't be the sum.

A.why: You took the other angle measure to be $90 - x$ (the complement) when it is really $180 - x$. With the complement, sums like $3x + (180 - x) = 180 + 2x$ seem impossible. In fact, three angles of $x^\circ$ plus one angle of $(180 - x)^\circ$ give exactly this sum.

B.why: You made a slip when you expanded $x + 3(180 - x)$, so $540 - 2x$ looked like it couldn't happen. One angle of $x^\circ$ plus three angles of $(180 - x)^\circ$ add up to exactly $540 - 2x$.

C.why: You assumed four angles can't add up to more than 360°, as if all four had to sit at the same crossing. The four angles that measure $(180 - x)^\circ$ are spread over both crossings, and together they add up to $720 - 4x$.

stimulus: On a town map, Main Street and Elm Street run east–west and are parallel. Elm Street lies south of Main Street. Route 9 is a straight road that crosses both streets. Where Route 9 meets Main Street, the angle on the south side of Main Street and the east side of Route 9 measures $(5x - 22)^\circ$. Where Route 9 meets Elm Street, the angle on the north side of Elm Street and the east side of Route 9 measures $(3x + 10)^\circ$.
explanation: Both angles lie between the two parallel streets, and both are on the east side of Route 9. That makes them same-side interior angles, so they add up to 180°. Solve $(5x - 22) + (3x + 10) = 180$: this gives $8x - 12 = 180$, so $8x = 192$ and $x = 24$.

A.why: You set the two angles equal, as if they were alternate interior angles: $5x - 22 = 3x + 10$ gives $x = 16$. Because they are on the same side of Route 9, they are supplementary, not equal.

C.why: You found $x = 24$ and then reported the Elm Street angle, $3(24) + 10 = 82$. The question asks for $x$.

D.why: You found $x = 24$ and then reported the Main Street angle, $5(24) - 22 = 98$. The question asks for $x$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of $\angle 3$?
stimulus: In a sports science lab, a researcher draws two straight lines on a frame of video, one along a sprinter's shin and one along the starting block. The lines cross at a single point and form four angles. Going clockwise around that point, the angles are labeled $\angle 1$, $\angle 2$, $\angle 3$, and $\angle 4$. The measure of $\angle 1$ is $(2x + 15)^\circ$ and the measure of $\angle 2$ is $(5x - 3)^\circ$.
explanation: $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ sit next to each other along one of the lines, so they form a linear pair and add up to 180°. Solve $(2x + 15) + (5x - 3) = 180$: this gives $7x = 168$, so $x = 24$ and $\angle 1 = 63^\circ$. $\angle 3$ is opposite $\angle 1$, so the two are vertical angles and $\angle 3 = 63^\circ$.

A.why: You solved correctly for $x = 24$ but stopped there. You still need to find the angle measure.

B.why: You set $\angle 1$ equal to $\angle 2$, as if they were vertical angles. That gives $x = 6$ and an angle of 27°. Neighboring angles on a line add up to 180°; they aren't equal.

D.why: You found 117°, which is the measure of $\angle 2$ and $\angle 4$. $\angle 3$ is opposite $\angle 1$, so it matches $\angle 1$ instead.

stimulus: A textile historian studying a woven twill cloth traces two parallel weft threads that run horizontally, one above the other. A straight diagonal twill line crosses both threads. At the upper thread, the angle above the thread and to the left of the diagonal measures $(x + 40)^\circ$. At the lower thread, the angle below the thread and to the right of the diagonal measures $(3x - 20)^\circ$.
explanation: Both angles lie outside the pair of parallel threads, and they are on opposite sides of the diagonal. That makes them alternate exterior angles, so they are equal. Solve $x + 40 = 3x - 20$: this gives $60 = 2x$, so $x = 30$.

B.why: You treated the angles as supplementary: $(x + 40) + (3x - 20) = 180$ gives $x = 40$. Alternate exterior angles are equal, not supplementary.

C.why: You found $x = 30$ and then reported the angle measure, $30 + 40 = 70$. The question asks for $x$.

D.why: You reported 110, which is the angle next to the 70° angle on the same line ($180 - 70$). That is neither $x$ nor either of the marked angles.

stem: Which of the following could be the sum of the measures, in degrees, of four of these eight angles?
stimulus: An ornithologist photographs a hawk gliding in a straight line across two parallel power lines. The glide path crosses both power lines and forms eight angles. One of the eight angles measures $64^\circ$.
explanation: A transversal across parallel lines makes only two angle measures: 64° and $180 - 64 = 116^\circ$. Four angles of each kind appear. The possible sums of four angles are $4(64) = 256$, $3(64) + 116 = 308$, $2(64) + 2(116) = 360$, $64 + 3(116) = 412$, and $4(116) = 464$. Only 412 is among the choices.

A.why: You took the other angle to be the complement, $90 - 64 = 26$, and added $3(64) + 26 = 218$. The other angle is the supplement, 116°.

B.why: You added only three angles: $64 + 2(116) = 296$. The question asks for the sum of four angles.

D.why: You added all four angles at one crossing (360°) and then another 64°. That is five angles, not four.
